title: Our ground-penetrating radar surveys on urban roads return raw B-scan images that our operators interpret visually; we miss about one in five utility pipes because operators disagree on what they see, and one missed gas pipe last year caused a major incident on a construction site.

record.text: Our ground-penetrating radar surveys on urban roads return raw B-scan images that our operators interpret visually; we miss about one in five utility pipes because operators disagree on what they see, and one missed gas pipe last year caused a major incident on a construction site.
record.detail: Every GPR survey on an urban road produces a stack of B-scan slices, and right now a trained operator sits down and draws lines on screen based on what looks like a hyperbola. Two operators looking at the same scan will sometimes disagree on whether a feature is a gas pipe, a water main, a cable duct, or just a tree root. We estimate we miss roughly one in five utilities this way, based on comparing our maps against later excavation findings on twenty completed projects over the past three years. Last spring a crew on a road-widening job in Subotica hit an undetected medium-pressure gas pipe; the incident shut the site for nine days and cost us and the contractor a combined settlement we do not want to repeat. We have tried stricter operator checklists and mandatory second-pass review, which helped a little but did not close the gap. We have raw B-scan files going back to 2017 on an internal server, roughly 4 terabytes, much of it from sites where the ground truth is now known from excavation. What we want is a reliable automated detection layer that flags probable pipe locations and gives the operator a confidence score, so disagreements can be escalated rather than silently dropped.
